Fabricate a data frame

Source: R/fabricate.R
fabricate.Rd

The main entry point for fabricatr. Builds a data frame column by column, supporting hierarchical levels, multi-column outputs, and starting from existing data.

Usage

fabricate(..., N = NULL, ID_label = "ID", data = NULL)

Arguments

...

Column definitions or level calls (add_level, nest_level, declare_level, import_level, cross_levels, link_levels, modify_level, potential_outcomes, draw_multivariate). N must be supplied by name.

N

Number of rows. Made available as a scalar integer N inside all column expressions; it does not appear as a column in the output unless you write it explicitly (e.g. n_obs = N).

ID_label

Name of the unit ID column created alongside N. Defaults to "ID"; set to NA to suppress it. Ignored when data is supplied or when the data frame is built from levels (each level's ID column is named after the level).

data

Optional existing data frame to start from.

Value

A tibble with one row per unit of the lowest level and columns in the order they were declared. Each level contributes an ID column named after the argument it was assigned to, placed before that level's own columns; a flat call contributes one named by ID_label, and ID_label = NA suppresses it. A call that starts from data adds no ID column at all. A nested level's IDs are unique across the whole frame rather than restarting inside each parent, so nesting 2 citizens in each of 3 villages numbers the citizens "1" through "6".

ID column type

ID columns are zero-padded character strings, as in fabricatr 1.x, so that an ID is a label rather than a quantity. The padding keeps character sort order matching numeric order, and the character type keeps a cluster ID from being read as a linear term by a model formula. The padding width is set by the number of units at that level, so a frame can hold clusters running "1" to "4" alongside units running "01" to "12".

Counting the rows a level is building

N names the number of rows the current level is building, so rnorm(N) draws one value per row. n() answers the same question as a function call and is available in every declaration. Two things make it worth reaching for. It cannot be confused with a parameter of the design: N is a name, so a design that also has an N in the workspace can leave a reader unsure which one an expression reads, and redesign() rebinds names, where n() always means the rows in hand. And a data set carrying a column called n keeps it: sum(n) reads the column and n() reads the count.

Examples

# Flat fabrication
fabricate(N = 100, Y = rnorm(N), X = rbinom(N, 1, 0.5))
#> # A tibble: 100 × 3
#>    ID          Y     X
#>    <chr>   <dbl> <int>
#>  1 001    0.290      1
#>  2 002    1.79       0
#>  3 003    0.341      1
#>  4 004   -0.242      1
#>  5 005    0.613      1
#>  6 006    0.0774     1
#>  7 007    1.78       0
#>  8 008    1.15       0
#>  9 009    0.732      1
#> 10 010   -0.642      1
#> # ℹ 90 more rows

# n() is the number of rows the level is building
fabricate(N = 10, Y = rnorm(n()))
#> # A tibble: 10 × 2
#>    ID          Y
#>    <chr>   <dbl>
#>  1 01    -0.941 
#>  2 02    -0.768 
#>  3 03    -0.0274
#>  4 04     0.103 
#>  5 05    -0.0119
#>  6 06     0.0767
#>  7 07     0.369 
#>  8 08    -0.205 
#>  9 09    -0.479 
#> 10 10     1.28  

# Hierarchical: 20 villages, 5 citizens each
fabricate(
  villages = add_level(N = 20, v_income = rnorm(N)),
  citizens = nest_level(N = 5, income = v_income + rnorm(N))
)
#> # A tibble: 100 × 4
#>    villages v_income citizens  income
#>    <chr>       <dbl> <chr>      <dbl>
#>  1 01          1.07  001       2.37  
#>  2 01          1.07  002       1.45  
#>  3 01          1.07  003       2.01  
#>  4 01          1.07  004       0.0224
#>  5 01          1.07  005       1.79  
#>  6 02          0.356 006      -2.25  
#>  7 02          0.356 007      -0.0328
#>  8 02          0.356 008      -0.276 
#>  9 02          0.356 009      -0.0298
#> 10 02          0.356 010       1.08  
#> # ℹ 90 more rows

# Starting from existing data
df <- data.frame(x = 1:10)
fabricate(data = df, y = x ^ 2)
#> # A tibble: 10 × 2
#>        x     y
#>    <int> <dbl>
#>  1     1     1
#>  2     2     4
#>  3     3     9
#>  4     4    16
#>  5     5    25
#>  6     6    36
#>  7     7    49
#>  8     8    64
#>  9     9    81
#> 10    10   100
